Raymond Chandler. An American writer living from eighteen eighty-eight to nineteen fifty-nine who transformed detective fiction by infusing it with hard-boiled authenticity, moral complexity, and literary sophistication. His novels featuring private detective Philip Marlowe depict a corrupt Los Angeles where crime permeates every social stratum and the detective himself is a morally ambiguous figure—tough, cynical, but driven by an obscure sense of justice. Chandler's prose is luminous and precise, and his dialogue crackles with wit and menace. He elevated detective fiction from pulp into serious literature and influenced generations of crime writers, filmmakers, and the emergence of noir as an aesthetic.

Philip Marlowe is Chandler's recurring protagonist: a Los Angeles private detective who navigates a corrupt landscape of wealthy criminals, compromised cops, and femmes fatales. Marlowe is tough but morally scrupulous, often protecting the guilty to serve a larger justice. The Big Sleep, published in nineteen thirty-nine, is Chandler's first novel and one of detective fiction's masterworks. It introduces Marlowe investigating a wealthy family's dark secrets. The plot is notoriously complicated, and Chandler himself was uncertain who committed one of the murders. Chandler's prose is distinguished by vivid metaphors, economical dialogue, and an unflinching gaze at urban corruption. One of his most famous openings reads, "It was a blonde. A blonde to make a bishop kick in a stained glass window."

His Los Angeles is not the glamorous city of tourist imagination but a sprawling, morally compromised landscape where wealth and power conceal systemic corruption and casual violence. Chandler moved into screenwriting and helped define the aesthetic of film noir, with his influence on cinema rivaling his impact on literature. He emphasized that detective fiction could achieve literary sophistication: strong characterization, moral complexity, and psychological depth alongside the mechanical necessities of plot. Hard-boiled detective fiction is unthinkable without Chandler. He is a foundational figure in the genre. Philip Marlowe appears in seven novels and numerous short stories. The Big Sleep is his debut and masterpiece, introducing Marlowe and establishing Chandler's style. Los Angeles is the setting for almost all his work, and Chandler depicted the city as a character and a moral landscape. His influence on film noir is substantial, with his novels adapted into classic noir films.
